t.sukhotai historical park@17.0,99.7:
In 1238, two Thai chiefs drove the Khmer governor out of a small city in the north of the central plain and founded a kingdom, and Sukhothai, the Dawn of Happiness, became the first capital of what we now call Thailand. The kingdom reached its height under King Ramkhamhaeng, who is credited with creating the Thai alphabet. A stone inscription dated to 1292, which is attributed to him, describes a country where there was fish in the water and rice in the fields, and where anyone with a grievance could ring a bell at the palace gate to be heard by the king. Whether the picture is wholly true is debated, but the image of a benevolent kingdom has clung to Sukhothai ever since.

The historical park, inscribed in 1991, is a wide, open area of ruins, lakes and lawns that is easy to explore by bicycle. The tall, slim chedis shaped like lotus buds, the broken columns of old halls, and the huge seated and walking Buddhas of Wat Mahathat, Wat Si Chum and Wat Sa Si make a peaceful, almost dreamlike landscape. At Wat Si Chum a giant seated Buddha, about fifteen metres high, is enclosed in a square walled chamber with a narrow slot, so that you see it first through a gap. The Sukhothai style, with its graceful, flowing walking Buddha, is regarded as the classic of Thai sculpture.

For riders the geography is easy, and the roads are some of the friendliest in the country. Highway 12 runs east to west across the plain, a wide, well-surfaced road with moderate traffic, while Highway 101 heads north to Si Satchanalai, the sister city, along a flat, pleasant road through rice fields and sugar cane. Motorcycles are everywhere in Thailand, and drivers expect them, but keep a careful eye out for pickups pulling out without warning, and dogs. The cool season, from November to February, is the best, with clear skies and light. March to May is very hot, and the rains of July to October bring fierce storms.

Sukhothai New City, about a dozen kilometres away, has plenty of fuel, markets and guesthouses, and Ban Na, closer, has services too. The town is famous for its noodle soup, with pork, peanuts and a dash of sweetness, and in November it holds the Loy Krathong festival, when candle-lit floats are set on the ponds.
t.chiang mai@18.8,99.0:
Chiang Mai rests in a broad valley in northern Thailand, ringed by mountains, and its old centre is a perfect square, bounded by a moat and the remains of brick walls. King Mengrai founded it in 1296 as the capital of the Lanna kingdom, a rich northern state with its own language, script and style of temple, and the old city still holds dozens of wats, glinting with gold leaf and carved teak. Doi Suthep, the mountain rising to the west, is crowned by a temple that is visible from the city at night.

Northern Thai culture has a distinct flavour. Khao soi, a curry noodle soup topped with crispy noodles, is the signature dish, and the city's night markets and Sunday walking street are full of crafts, textiles and street food. Mornings start early with monks collecting alms, and the air smells of charcoal, jasmine and frying garlic. The city has a relaxed pace, and many travellers stay longer than planned.

The Mae Hong Son Loop is the reason riders gather here. It is famous for its curves, often quoted as 1,864 in total on the main route, winding through forested mountains, rice terraces and hill-tribe villages. The road climbs to Doi Inthanon, Thailand's highest peak at 2,565 metres, where the air is cool and mossy cloud forest clings to the slopes. Surfaces are generally good, though rain can leave mud and gravel on bends. Be careful of buses and trucks cutting corners and of dogs and chickens on the road. The cool season from November to February is best, with clear skies. From about February to April, farmers burn fields and the haze can be thick and unhealthy, and the rainy months from June to October bring afternoon downpours.

Chiang Mai has everything a rider needs: motorbike rental shops, mechanics, fuel at every main road, and endless guesthouses and cafes. Hang Dong, south of the city, is the usual exit for the loop. Pack rain gear, carry your licence and an international permit, and always wear a helmet, because police checks are common. Fill up before the hills, where stations are fewer.
t.kamphaeng phet historical park@16.5,99.5:
Kamphaeng Phet means diamond wall, though the name probably refers to the strength of the fortifications rather than to any gems. The historical park lies on the Ping river in the lower north of Thailand, a short ride from a provincial town of nearly sixty thousand, and it protects the remains of a city that served as a fortress of the Sukhothai kingdom in the fourteenth century. Together with Sukhothai itself and Si Satchanalai, it makes up a UNESCO World Heritage group that records the first great Thai kingdom.

The ruins are made of laterite, the reddish, porous stone that was quarried locally, and many are covered with moss and the roots of old trees. Rows of columns stand in the grass, the remains of halls, and big seated Buddhas rest in the shade of the forest, some with their heads missing and some still serene. Wat Phra Kaeo, the temple of the Emerald Buddha in the old days, has a row of chedi and a tall standing figure, and the temple of the elephants, Wat Chang Rop, has a base surrounded by sculpted elephants, which look as if they are carrying the monument on their backs. Walls and moats of the city can still be traced.

The park is sprawling, with the main groups inside the old town and others in the forest to the north, and the best way to see it is to ride slowly from one temple to the next, or hire a bicycle. Paths are mostly paved, with some bumpy sections. Heat is the main enemy, with temperatures regularly above thirty-five degrees, so go early or late, wear a hat and carry water. The rainy season, from June to October, brings sudden downpours and thick green growth.

The road from Sukhothai, about eighty kilometres to the north, is straight, flat and fast, with long views over rice fields and the occasional town. Kamphaeng Phet has fuel stations, noodle shops, a night market and simple hotels, and the town's river promenade is a pleasant place to sit as the sun goes down.

Visit between November and February for the coolest weather, and linger at sunset, when the laterite glows.
t.mae hong son@19.3,98.0:
Mae Hong Son sits at the end of one of the best-known motorcycle journeys in Thailand, in a bowl of hills right up against the Myanmar border. The town is small, with about nine thousand residents, and its southern and western streets are overlooked by mountains that trap fog in the cool season. Locals call it the city of three mists, and on a December morning you can ride out of town into a world where the lake and temples float on white cloud.

The best known road here is the loop from Chiang Mai through Pai, the route that is advertised as having close to two thousand curves. Most riders take it by way of Highway 1095, which twists over forested ridges from Pai, climbing and falling constantly. Surfaces are good, but corners come fast, with gravel, wet leaves and the odd stray dog or truck on the wrong side. Take your time. The reward is views of layered hills that fade into blue haze, and the pleasure of rolling into town as the afternoon light turns gold.

The town shows its Shan heritage, the people known as Tai Yai in Thailand, who came from across the border. Two temples beside Chong Kham lake, Wat Chong Kham and Wat Chong Klang, have the white and gold stupas and tiered roofs of Burmese style, and in the evening they are reflected in the water. On a hill above town, Wat Phra That Doi Kong Mu looks over the valley, and it is a favourite place to watch the sunrise breaking above the mist. In the morning the market sells Shan noodles and sticky rice snacks.

Fuel is easy in town, but the mountain roads between Pai and Mae Hong Son are long, so top up before the climb. The cool season from November to February is the best time, with clear skies and crisp air. In the hot months from March to April, farmers burn their fields and smoke settles in the valleys, and in the rainy season from June to October, landslides and mud can close sections of road, although the hills turn intensely green. Hotels and guesthouses are plentiful, so the rider's evening is usually decided by how tired the arms are.
t.mae rim@18.9,98.9:
Mae Rim is the northern gate of Chiang Mai, a sprawling town about fifteen kilometres from the old city, where the Ping river valley narrows and the hills begin. The Mae Sa valley runs west from here, and it holds waterfalls, orchid farms, butterfly houses and elephant camps, as well as a road that winds up through the forest toward the Samoeng loop. It is the sort of place that tourists find in a day and riders find for a lifetime.

For riders, Mae Rim is the start of something big. Highway 107 runs north toward Chiang Dao and the Burmese border, and farther on, Highway 1095 branches off toward Pai and Mae Hong Son, a long mountain route that has become famous for its endless bends. Riders talk about the Mae Hong Son loop in hundreds of curves, and the numbers are no exaggeration. Fuel is plentiful here, with big stations along the main road and plenty of small shops, but stations become farther apart once you climb, so it is best to fill up before you head into the hills.

Chiang Mai itself was founded in 1296 by King Mengrai as capital of the Lanna kingdom, and the old city still has its moat and brick walls, with temples at every turn. The food of the north is distinct from that of Bangkok, with khao soi, a curry noodle soup topped with crispy noodles, as the signature dish. Sai oua, a spicy herbal sausage, and sticky rice are staples, and a bowl of khao soi at a roadside stall makes a fine breakfast before the climb.

The climate matters. From November to February, the air is cool and dry, and the mornings can be cold in the hills. From March to May, smoke from agricultural burning fills the valleys with haze, and the air can be unpleasant. The rainy season, from June to October, brings green hills, but also landslides and slippery roads. Choose your season with care.

Check the bike, fill the tank, eat well and go early. The hills are waiting.
t.doi inthanon junction@18.6,98.5:
At about two and a half thousand metres Doi Inthanon is the highest point in Thailand, and the road to the top is one of the few in the country where you will be wearing a jacket in the tropics. The mountain is the southern end of the Himalayan chain, and its slopes are covered by forest that changes with height, from teak and bamboo at the bottom through oak and pine to a cloud forest dripping with moss, orchids and tree ferns.

The road from Chom Thong climbs steadily, with a long series of curves, past waterfalls such as Mae Klang and Wachirathan, which throw a cooling mist across the tarmac, and through hill-tribe villages where Karen and Hmong farmers grow coffee and cabbages on terraced fields. The surface is good and well maintained, and the bends are open and smooth, but fog and rain can arrive suddenly. A fee is charged for entering the national park, and motorcycles pay a small amount. The top is often cold, sometimes close to freezing in the dry season, so wear layers.

Near the summit you will find two chedis, or pagodas, built by the Thai air force to mark the sixtieth birthdays of the king and the queen, set in a garden with views across the mountains. In the cool season, the gardens are full of flowers. A short boardwalk, the Ang Ka Nature Trail, loops through the cloud forest and a small bog, and it is a gentle, atmospheric walk. Birdwatchers come from all over the world to look for the rare species that live up here, from sunbirds to the green-tailed sunbird.

The best time is the cool season, from November to February, when the air is clear and the views reach far. The rainy season, from June to October, brings mist and slippery roads. Stalls near the top sell hot drinks, grilled corn and strawberries, and little noodle shops serve warming soup. This is the finish of a long climb, so take your time at the summit, drink something hot, and enjoy having reached the roof of the country.
t.chiang rai@19.9,99.8:
Chiang Rai lies on the Kok river in the far north of Thailand, a calm, tidy provincial city that has the foothills of the Shan Plateau on one side and the broad plain on the other. It was founded in 1262 by King Mengrai, who went on to found Chiang Mai too, and the old Lanna kingdom left a distinct culture, with its own script, its own cooking and its own temple style. The clock tower in the centre, a gold and white confection, lights up in changing colours every evening, and the night bazaar is a pleasant spot for a bowl of khao soi, curried noodles topped with crispy noodles, the dish of the north.

The city's most famous sight is Wat Rong Khun, the White Temple, a dazzling creation of the artist Chalermchai Kositpipat, begun in 1997, with white plaster and mirror glass and gates guarded by hands reaching up from hell. It is flamboyant, sometimes odd, and always crowded, so go early. The Blue Temple, Wat Rong Suea Ten, offers a quieter, colourful alternative.

The rides from here are glorious. North, the road runs to the Golden Triangle at Sop Ruak, where the Mekong forms the border of Thailand, Laos and Myanmar, a historic crossroads of the opium trade. West, a steep road climbs to Doi Mae Salong, a mountain village founded by Chinese Nationalist soldiers who fled after 1949, where terraced tea gardens produce oolong, and the cool air feels like another country. The road has many tight hairpins and steep gradients, but the surface is generally good. Fog and rain can come at any time, and the heat in the lowlands in March and April is intense, with smoke from burning fields.

Fuel is plentiful in Chiang Rai and on the main roads, but mountain villages have fewer pumps, so fill the tank beforehand. The best time to ride is from November to February, when the air is cool and the skies are clear.
t.pai mountain road@19.4,98.4:
Pai is a small valley town in the mountains of Mae Hong Son province, in the north-west corner of Thailand, and it has a reputation that far outweighs its size. A few thousand people live here, at a bend in the Pai River, and in the last few decades the place has attracted travellers, artists and musicians who stayed for a while and never quite left. The result is a mixture of old Shan and Yunnanese Chinese culture, backpacker cafes and a night market that sells everything from fried insects to handmade jewellery.

The road to Pai is part of the legend. Route 1095, which comes up from Mae Malai, is said to have over seven hundred bends in about a hundred kilometres, and riders count them, or claim to. The road climbs through teak forest and over a ridge before dropping into the valley, and it is a splendid ride, with well-made tarmac and a lot of traffic of its own. The corners are tight, the gradients steady, and the minibuses full of tourists take them fast, so watch for blind corners and for vehicles cutting across the line. Road accidents are common here, and helmets are essential.

Near the town, the Pai Canyon is a ridge of narrow clay ridges with steep drops on each side, and people gather there at sunset. A short ride to the hot springs at Tha Pai is a good way to ease sore muscles. Wat Phra That Mae Yen sits on a hill above the town, with a long stairway and a view across the valley. The valley itself is green, with rice fields and tobacco, and in the cool season, morning mist sits low among the trees.

Pai has a gentle climate between November and February, with cool mornings and warm afternoons. The rainy season, from May to October, brings downpours and landslides on the road, and the hot season, in March and April, is often smoky from burning in the fields and forests. The best time to ride is the cool season, with the clearest air.

Fuel is available in town, and there are many cafes, restaurants and guesthouses. Ask around for a reliable bike mechanic if you need one, as there are a few. A bowl of khao soi, the northern curry noodles, is the local dish to try.
t.doi inthanon option@18.6,98.5:
Doi Inthanon is the highest mountain in Thailand, at 2,565 metres, and the road to the top is a pleasure for anyone who likes to climb. From Chom Thong, a market town on the plain, Route 1009 winds up through the national park, passing waterfalls, villages and layers of forest, and reaching a summit that is cold, damp and often wrapped in cloud. Temperatures at the top can fall close to freezing on winter nights, a surprise for a country known for heat, and it is wise to pack a warm layer.

The mountain is the southern end of the Himalayan chain's outliers, and the forest on its upper slopes is a rare habitat, a cloud forest where moss hangs from every branch and ferns and orchids cover the trees. Birdwatchers love it, and it holds more than three hundred species, including some found nowhere else in Thailand. The Ang Ka nature trail, near the summit, is a short boardwalk through a mossy forest. Two large pagodas near the top were built by the Royal Thai Air Force to honour the king and queen, and the gardens around them are bright with flowers.

Karen and Hmong people live on the mountain, and their villages grow coffee, strawberries and vegetables on terraces. Waterfalls fall in tiers on the way up, and the largest, Wachirathan and Mae Ya, are worth a stop. After rain, they thunder, and the spray is cool on a hot day. The summit has a small marker and a spot of national pride, and in the cool season, a crowd gathers to watch the sunrise.

The ride up is steady, with good tarmac, some steep ramps and many bends, and few straight stretches. The road is narrow near the top and traffic can be heavy at weekends. Take it slowly, because fog and rain can reduce visibility quickly, and the road can be slippery. The park charges an entry fee, which includes the motorbike. Early starts are best, before cloud builds and the tour buses arrive.

Services on the mountain are limited, with small restaurants and stalls near the summit, but fuel is a matter for the plain. Chom Thong, about twenty-seven kilometres away, has stations and food. Fill up there, and bring cash and a jacket.
t.si satchanalai historical park@17.4,99.8:
Si Satchanalai is the quieter sibling of Sukhothai, and many riders prefer it for exactly that reason. It sits on the Yom River in northern Thailand's lower north, in a bowl of low hills, and what remains of the old city is spread across a park of trimmed lawns, laterite walls and big shade trees. The kingdom of Sukhothai used this as a sister city in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and the monuments here, in a style that mixes Khmer, Sinhalese and Thai ideas, are some of the earliest Thai Buddhist architecture you can still walk among.

The most striking shapes are the chedi at Wat Chang Lom, the elephant-ringed temple whose bell-shaped stupa stands on a square base held up by thirty-nine stone elephants, and the ridge-top Wat Khao Phanom Phloeng, from which the whole valley is laid out like a map. Climb there in late afternoon when the heat softens. Nearby, the old kiln sites made the glazed celadon known as Sawankhalok ware, shipped across Southeast Asia long before Europeans arrived.

The riding in the lower north is not dramatic but it is pleasant. Highway 101 and the smaller roads along the Yom run through rice flats, teak plantations and fruit orchards on gently rolling land. The tarmac is good and wide, the bends are mild, and the main hazards are trucks, dogs, and sudden flocks of schoolchildren on bicycles. Temperatures are fierce between March and May, comfortable from November to February, and in the rainy season the afternoon storms arrive on schedule, so aim to ride in the morning.

The park has cycle hire, which is how most people cover it, and stalls at the entrance sell noodles, coconut ice cream and iced coffee. Si Satchanalai town is about eleven kilometres away and big enough to have fuel, a market and basic lodging, while Sawankhalok, a little further, has more choice, and Uttaradit is the nearest proper city. A ticket is required at the main gates, usually with a separate fee for riding a motorbike inside. Bring a hat and water, since shade between the monuments is thinner than you hope.
t.pai@19.4,98.4:
Pai is a small town in a green bowl of hills in the far north-west of Thailand, near the Burmese border, and it has been a backpacker retreat for decades. The Pai river winds through a valley of rice paddies and tobacco fields at about five hundred metres, and the mountains around it hold bamboo huts, hot springs, waterfalls and the villages of Shan, Lisu, Lahu and Chinese Yunnanese communities. The town itself is a cheerful tangle of guesthouses, bars, cafes and craft shops, with a night market along the walking street, where stalls sell grilled corn, fruit shakes, noodles and handmade bags.

Getting here is the first challenge. The road from Chiang Mai, Highway 1095, is famous for its twisting curves, and a sign on the way proudly claims there are 762 of them. It climbs over a mountain pass, running through hardwood forest and past viewpoints with coffee stalls, and the bends are tight, steady and often tree-shaded. The surface is generally good, but there are patches of loose gravel, and heavy rain brings mud and slips. Scooters are common, and so are accidents, so pace yourself and ride defensively, as the road is shared with trucks, buses and tourists on rented bikes.

Pai has some quiet local history. The Pai Memorial Bridge, a steel structure on the edge of town, recalls the Second World War, when Japanese troops passed through the area. On a hill above town sits Wat Phra That Mae Yen, a white Buddhist temple reached by a long staircase of 353 steps, with a view across the valley, best at sunset. Pai Canyon, a maze of narrow ridges of eroded earth, is another sunset spot, though the edges are not fenced, so take care.

The best season is November to February, when the air is cool and clear, mornings are misty and the hills are green after the rains. From late February to April, farmers burn their fields across northern Thailand and the valley fills with smoke, which can be hard on the lungs and spoils the view. The rainy season, from June to October, makes the road slippery, though the waterfalls are at their best.

There is fuel in town, as well as repair shops, pharmacies and plenty of food, from northern Thai sausage and khao soi curry noodles to simple Western breakfasts. It is a place to relax for a day or two, before taking the road on toward Mae Hong Son.
t.mae sariang@18.2,97.9:
Mae Sariang is a quiet river town in the far west of Thailand, with Myanmar a short ride away over the hills. It sits on the Yuam River, wedged between the Thanon Thong Chai range to the east and the mountains along the Salween to the west, and the feel is of a place at the edge of things. The people here are largely Karen, along with Shan and Thai, and the markets sell sticky rice, pickled tea leaves and bundles of fresh vegetables brought down from the hills. Burmese-style temples with tiered roofs and white stupas recall the teak trade, when Burmese and Shan timber workers came to cut the forests and left their religion and their architecture behind.

The riding is the real treat. Highway 108 runs up from Chiang Mai through Hot and Mae Chaem, climbs and falls over forested ridges, and arrives at Mae Sariang after hours of curves. It is a smooth, well-kept road with a tight rhythm of bends and gentle climbs, with long stretches of teak and bamboo forest and views across hazy valleys. The Mae Hong Son loop is famous for having nearly two thousand curves, and this section does its fair share. Mist hangs in the valleys in the cool season, and the air smells of woodsmoke and rain.

The season matters. From November to February the mornings are cool and clear and the riding is superb. From March to April the hills are covered in smoke from agricultural burning, which hides the views and is unpleasant to breathe, and the rainy season from June to October brings landslides and slick surfaces. Fuel is easy, since Mae Sariang is a proper town with petrol stations, guesthouses and a good supply of noodle shops and cafes, and a stop for the night here is common.

The river is the town's centre. Guesthouses with decks hang over the water, and a long evening with a cold drink and a bowl of noodles is a pleasant reward after a day in the saddle. Nearby, the Salween River forms the border with Myanmar at Mae Sam Laep, a day trip along a winding road, where long-tail boats shuttle up and down the wide brown water.

The Karen villages in the hills, with their wooden houses on stilts, keep elephants and tend terraced fields, and courteous visitors are generally welcome. Slow down through the settlements, because children, dogs and chickens treat the road as common ground.
t.historic town of sukhothai and associate:
Sukhothai was the first capital of a Thai kingdom, and the name means Dawn of Happiness. In the thirteenth century, two Thai chieftains drove out the Khmer governors and founded a state here, and under King Ramkhamhaeng, who ruled in the late thirteenth century, it grew into a power across much of the region. Tradition credits him with creating the Thai alphabet and with an inscription describing a golden age, where there was fish in the water and rice in the fields. The kingdom was short-lived, absorbed by Ayutthaya in the fifteenth century, but Sukhothai is remembered as the cradle of Thai art, religion and identity.

The historical park is a spacious place of lotus ponds, grassy lawns and brick and laterite ruins, with the large temple of Wat Mahathat at its heart. The Buddha figures of Sukhothai are famous for their elegance, with soft, flowing lines and a smile of calm. In the park, hire a bicycle and ride between the monuments at your own pace. The slender, lotus-bud towers and the walking Buddha in relief are signatures of the style. The place is lovely at sunrise and sunset, when the stone glows and the heat drops. Wat Si Chum, a short ride away, shelters a huge seated Buddha in a high-walled chamber, and its face seems to look right at you.

Sukhothai is also linked to the festival of Loy Krathong, held on the full moon in November, when people float small lotus-shaped boats of banana leaf with candles on rivers and ponds. The festival is said to have started here, and the town puts on a big celebration with fireworks and performances.

The wider listing includes the town of Kamphaeng Phet to the south, and the ride between them is a pleasant one on Highway 101 across flat, green rice country, with palms and small villages. The road is smooth, with light traffic, and the heat is the main issue, so start early. The new town of Sukhothai, a dozen kilometres east of the park, has fuel stations, hotels and restaurants, and the old town has a handful of guesthouses and cafes. Try the local noodles, served in a sweet-sour broth with pork and morning glory.

The cool season, from November to February, is the best time for riding and for the ruins.
t.mae hong son loop point 5@18.6,98.5:
Doi Inthanon is the highest mountain in Thailand, at 2,565 metres, and the road to its summit is a ride into another climate. The air cools by ten degrees or more as you climb, the forest changes from tropical to a dripping cloud forest of moss, orchids and tree ferns, and at the top the temperature can drop close to freezing on winter nights. Chom Thong, the town at the foot, is where most riders turn off the main road, and Chiang Mai lies roughly a hundred kilometres to the north-east.

The road up is a good one, narrow and steep, with plenty of bends and a surface of tarmac that is generally good, though it can be slippery with mist. Two royal pagodas stand on a ridge near the summit, built to honour the King and Queen on their sixtieth birthdays, with gardens full of flowers. At the very top, a short walk leads to a shrine where the ashes of the last prince of Chiang Mai are kept, and a sign marking the highest point in the country.

The park is known for its bird life, and bird watchers come from all over the world to see its rarities. The Wachirathan waterfall, beside the road, falls in a thick, noisy sheet, and in the cool air it throws up a mist that drifts across the tarmac. Hill tribe villages of Hmong and Karen on the lower slopes grow coffee and vegetables, and fruit stalls along the road sell strawberries and peaches in the cool season.

There is an entrance fee for the national park, and a checkpoint near the base. Fuel is not sold on the mountain, so fill up in Chom Thong. A few food stalls and a small restaurant serve the visitors, and the market near the pagodas sells hot drinks. The road is open all year, but in the rainy season, fog and rain reduce visibility, and in the cool season, from November to February, the mornings can be very cold. Bring a jacket and gloves.
t.near ban huai i huak@18.2,97.9:
Mae Sariang is where the Mae Hong Son Loop takes a breath. Coming from Chiang Mai on Route 108, you have spent the morning winding up through Hot and over a long, forested ridge, and then the road drops into the valley of the Yuam River and this small, unhurried market town appears, the first proper town in a long while.

It has a different feel from the Thai lowlands. This is close to the Myanmar border, and the population is a mix of Thai, Shan, Karen and other hill peoples, with a strong Burmese influence visible in the temples: tiered roofs of wood and corrugated metal, white chedis and Shan-style decoration. The river runs past the edge of town, and in the evening people walk along it and eat at the small restaurants on the bank. West of town, a road runs to Mae Sam Laep on the Salween River, which forms the border, and the Salween National Park protects the forested hills on the Thai side.

For riders, the road south and north of Mae Sariang is what the loop is all about. Route 108 is mostly smooth asphalt with endless curves as it climbs over the hills, with long stretches through teak forest and bamboo, steep gradients and tight corners. North of Mae Sariang the road becomes even more twisting as it heads toward Khun Yuam and Mae Hong Son, with fewer villages and more empty forest. In the rainy season, from roughly June to October, landslides and potholes are common, and the surface can be slippery. In the cool season, from November to February, the riding is at its best, with clear skies and cool mornings, though the hills can be shrouded in mist until mid-morning.

Mae Sariang has everything you need: fuel stations, small hotels and guesthouses, markets, restaurants and cafes. It is a good place to spend a night, especially if you want to break the loop into shorter stages. The local food is worth trying: khao soi, the northern curry noodle soup, is everywhere, and Shan dishes such as tua nao, fermented soybean, are a speciality of the region. Fill up here before heading north, since the gaps between towns with proper fuel stations get longer.
